How this is picked: 62 cars passed today, out of every clean used Model 3 and Model Y we can see. A car must have no accidents, a clean title, under 60,000 miles, a healthy battery, at least 3 years and 40,000 miles of battery warranty left, and a seller rated 4.0 stars or higher. Then each car is ranked by real savings: what Tesla would normally ask for that year, trim and mileage, minus what it costs you to get it home after any Illinois rebate. Dealer cars also take a $1,000 charge because they lack Tesla's used-car warranty. Sales tax and fees are not included, and trip costs are estimates.

The short answer: buy a 2023 Tesla from Tesla's own used inventory. Don't lease.

The federal tax credit is gone, so leases are no longer subsidized, and the Illinois $2,000 rebate only pays if you buy. A clean 2024 Model 3 from Tesla's Libertyville store costs $31,700 (about $29,700 after the Illinois rebate), still has years of battery coverage, and Tesla adds its own 1-year/10,000-mile used warranty. Clean dealer 2021 to 2023 Model 3s run $22,300 to $24,900, and clean Model Ys start near $23,000. A new Model Y Standard is $41,630 and loses roughly $8,000 the first year, which is money the 2023 owner already lost for you.

Shopping on a tight budget? The Under $15k tab ranks the cheapest Teslas in the country by price for battery left (dollars per mile of range). Pick the tab for the car you want, or the combined power rank to see both models head to head. Each list has its own benchmark: the #1 deal on that list sets the bar, every other deal shows its score against it, and cars that meet or beat the bar turn yellow.

When to buy

The short version: be ready now, buy the day a car on this page meets your bar, and do not let an Illinois purchase slip past December 31.

  • Illinois $2,000 rebate. The current cycle closes December 31, 2026 . It covers used electric cars but only from a dealer licensed in Illinois, and it pays as funding allows. Confirm with the dealer in writing before signing, and apply right away.
  • Tesla's year-end push. Tesla discounted hardest in late December last year, with 0% financing on new cars. Whether that reaches used cars is still unproven: nothing in our tracking so far shows a calendar effect on used prices.
  • Used-car seasons. Sources disagree between November and January as the best month. See the History + when to buy tab.

Before you need it: get a credit-union pre-approval and your Jeep offers lined up, so you can move the day the right car shows up.

Reality check from the daily log (Nov 12): the typical asking price has gone UP about 2.7% since Oct 25, so waiting has cost money so far. Single cars do get cheaper every day they sit, then sell, and a fresh car takes the spot at a fresh price. So the deal comes from catching one car late in its cuts, in any week. The cut clock on each Tesla-store car, and the table on the Power rank tab, show the odds.

Can't-say-no watch

Why $55 per mile of range: a new Model Y Standard costs about $130 for each mile of range, a 3-year-old Tesla from Tesla about $100 to $140, and the cheapest high-mile cars about $40 to $60. Paying $55 or less means getting range at well under half the new-car price; pairing it with battery warranty keeps worn-out cars from winning.

Nothing clears the can't-say-no bar today. You will see a green YES here (and get a phone alert) the day something does.

The cut clock: how long cars last, and is waiting paying off?

Tesla prices its used cars like a clearance rack. Almost every car is cut a little every day until someone buys it. Then a fresh car takes its place at a fresh, higher price. 18 days of logging every clean Tesla-store Model 3 and Model Y (since Oct 25) show how the clock runs. Every Tesla-store car on this board now carries its own cut clock line.

Price todayTypical cutGone by the next dayHalf are gone withinTotal cut by the time it was gone (cars we saw arrive)

What to do with this. Do not fall for one exact car and wait on it: most are sold within a week. Know your price instead (each row shows its can't-say-no price) and take the first clean car that reaches it. The cars worth watching are the ones already deep into their cuts: they sit on the markdown lists above. December 15 to 31 still matters for the Illinois rebate and for Tesla's year-end offers. If the typical price starts to slide before then, this table will show it first.

Raise tracker: when Tesla raises a car, should you wait?

Tesla raised 581 clean used cars by $500 or more since logging began (typically $1,100). Of the 559 raises that are at least 3 days old, 47% fell back to the old price or lower while the car was still for sale (the typical one took 3 days). The rest were sold at the higher price or are still waiting. So a raise is not a signal to hold out for the old price: if a raised car still clears your can't-say-no price, decide on it, and if not, move on to the next one.

Tesla cut more cars than it raised on 6 of the last 7 days. Each row compares every clean Tesla-store car with its own price the day before. If cuts keep winning into December, waiting for the December 15 to 31 window costs you little; if raises start winning, buy sooner.

Best price for the miles and battery left

All 33 used Teslas on this board, every model and price, ranked on what you get for your money in both ways a used Tesla wears out. Battery: the price for each mile of range the battery should give today. Miles: the price for each 1,000 miles of driving life left, counting a Tesla as good for about 300,000 miles or 20 years, whichever comes first, driving about 12,000 miles a year (so an old car with low miles still loses life to age). Each car gets a score out of 100 on both (100 = the best on the board) and the value score is the average of the two, so a cheap car with worn-out miles and a pricey low-mile car both lose to one that is good on both. #1 is the benchmark and anything within 5% of it is yellow. Only cars.com dealers rated 4.0 stars or higher, and Tesla's own stores.

Every deal we have tracked, and what it says about timing

What this covers: this board began October 11 and has logged every clean Tesla-store car daily since October 25. That is 18 days of full data, not a full year, so it cannot show spring or summer prices yet. It grows every day.

Waiting has not paid so far. The typical 2023 Model Y Long Range went from $36,600 to $37,700, and the typical 2023 Model 3 RWD from $28,700 to $30,900. Single cars get cut, then sell, and new cars arrive at higher prices.
The best deals come in short bursts. The best day was Oct 28 at 15.0% below Tesla's usual price. A discount of 12% or more showed up on 14 of 18 days, usually on only one to three cars. Of the best cars that have sold, the typical one was gone 7 days after we first saw it.
Dealers often beat Tesla. Clean cars at 4.0-star-plus dealers typically cost $1,506 to $4,083 less than Tesla asks for the same year, trim and miles. Tesla's used-car warranty is what you give up.

Under $15,000: ranked by price for battery left

From every used Tesla listed on cars.com nationwide between $9,000 and $15,000 with under 120,000 miles (rechecked every day), keeping only cars.com Great and Good Deals from dealers rated 4.0 stars or higher, with no accidents reported in their history (checked on each listing; cars with a reported accident are left off). "Range score" is cars.com's battery-health rating, built from real driving data for that model: Good means the battery has held up about as well as most; Fair means noticeably weaker. Battery warranty is 8 years from the car's first sale, capped at 100,000 miles (Standard Range) or 120,000 (Long Range); every 2013 to 2016 Model S is past it.

How to judge a used Tesla battery

Ask the seller for a photo of the screen at a 100% charge, shown in miles, and divide it by the range when new (listed on every car below). Tesla batteries lose most of their capacity early, then fade slowly: Tesla reports about 12% average loss at 200,000 miles on Model S and X, and early Model 3 data shows under 10% at 100,000. Many reach 200,000 miles on the original battery; 300,000 is possible with noticeably less range.

Range left vs. newRatingWhat it means
90% or moreExcellentBetter than typical for its miles
85% to 90%GoodNormal for 80,000 to 150,000 miles
80% to 85%FairUsable; the price should reflect it
Under 80%AvoidUnless very cheap and you only drive short trips

These bands are a rule of thumb built from Tesla's fleet data and real high-mileage cars, not an official scale. The "expect today" numbers on each car assume normal wear for its miles, minus a little for 2013 to 2016 cars (age) and more for cars cars.com rates Fair. Winter range assumes about 30% less in a Chicago January. Other checks: Tesla's built-in battery health test (Service menu on newer software) or a Recurrent report, and steer clear of ex-Uber or ex-taxi cars that lived on fast chargers unless the range number checks out.

How these are ranked: price divided by the range the battery should give today (the "expect about" numbers in each car's battery check). Lower is better: it is what you pay for each mile of battery left. The #1 car is the benchmark; any car within 5% of it is also yellow. Ranks use the listed price; the Illinois $2,000 rebate is noted on the Illinois car.

The honest picture: at this price you are choosing between a 2019 to 2022 Model 3 with about 90,000 to 110,000 miles, or a 2013 to 2016 Model S with lower miles but no warranty and expensive repairs (an out-of-warranty Model S battery or drive unit can cost more than the car). For most people the Model 3 is the safer buy. Nearly all of these are far away: the only two within an hour score just Fair on battery.

Before you buy any of these: ask the dealer for a battery health report (Recurrent or a Tesla service printout), check that the car's screen shows the full expected range at 100% charge, run the VIN on Tesla's site for open recalls, and on any Model S ask whether it still has free Supercharging. Illinois-dealer cars get the $2,000 state rebate; out-of-state cars do not.

Cybercab watch

Can you buy one? Not yet, and probably not in 2026. As of November 11, 2026 there is still no order page, reservation or price for buyers (Tesla only has a fleet-operator inquiry form), and no new NHTSA ruling turned up.

Latest (November 6): still nothing to buy, but Tesla is betting its Texas factory on this car. Musk said this week that Cybertruck production in Texas will wind down around the middle of 2027 to make room for more Cybercabs. That tells you Tesla is serious about building them in volume. It does not tell you when, or whether, you can own one: there is still no price, no order page and no federal sign-off. The Europe show tour that began November 5 is look-only, and Tesla has still not given a firm date for rides in Dallas.

Federal audit (updated November 5): Tesla met NHTSA's October 30 deadline and filed its sworn answers to the 21 questions about how it certified a car with no steering wheel or pedals as legal to sell. It then asked NHTSA to keep the whole file secret as confidential business information. The only public piece is a guide for firefighters. NHTSA's lawyers now decide whether that secrecy holds and can order a public version; there is no deadline. This is a response, not an approval: the audit stays open, and NHTSA has not said the car fails either. Tesla skipped the exemption route Zoox used, which caps sales at 2,500 cars a year, and certified the car itself. Until NHTSA accepts that, nobody can buy one.

Federal regulators, the back story: on September 10 NHTSA ordered Tesla to prove, under oath, that the Cybercab meets federal safety rules; Tesla asked for eight extra weeks and got 30 days. Nothing new on pricing, an order page, or Illinois approval.

What Tesla said this week: on its October 21 earnings call, a Tesla engineering vice president said they are "trying" to get Cybercabs to customers by the end of 2026. That is a goal, not a delivery schedule. On the same call Musk said most Cybercabs will be owned by Tesla and run as its own ride service, so early cars may never be sold to individuals at all.

Where it stands: production started at Tesla's Texas factory in April. Paid Cybercab rides started in Austin in early September, by invitation, and Tesla says more cities before year end. Price: Musk keeps saying "under $30,000"; Tesla has published nothing.

Why it is not close for you: it has no steering wheel or pedals, so it can only be sold to the public with a federal exemption (NHTSA proposed a rule change for driverless designs on October 23; a proposal is not approval), and you could only use it where Tesla's unsupervised self-driving is allowed. Today that is a handful of Texas and West Coast cities, not Illinois. Earning money with it also needs Tesla to open its ride network to owners, which it has promised but not done.

What to do: buy the best-value used Tesla now, and treat the Cybercab as a possible second car in 2027 or later. I will flag the day an order page opens.

Model Y or Model 3 for you?

Short answer: get a Long Range AWD (all-wheel drive) either way. Rear-drive Teslas are weaker on Illinois snow and ice, and the Long Range cars also hold more battery.

Model Y: taller seat, easier to climb in and out, a hatchback with far more cargo room (about 76 cubic feet with the seats folded, versus roughly 20 for the Model 3 trunk plus front trunk). Costs about $1,000 to $3,000 more than a Model 3 of the same year and miles, and the ride is a bit firmer on 20-inch wheels.

Model 3: cheaper, sportier, a little farther per charge on the same battery because it is lower and lighter, and the sedan trunk is fine for groceries and luggage but not for bulky items.

Rule of thumb: if you ever haul bikes, big boxes or luggage for a family, pay the extra for the Model Y. If it is mostly you and a passenger, the Model 3 is the better dollar. Both use the same charging network and the same winter range loss (about 25 to 30 percent in January).

Before you buy

  • Illinois rebate: $2,000 back on a used or new EV, bought from an Illinois-licensed dealer (Tesla's Illinois stores qualify; ask for delivery through an Illinois location on an out-of-state car). The window is open now through December 31, 2026, or until the $14 million runs out. You apply after purchase, within 180 days. Household income must be under 500% of the federal poverty line, which is about $160,000 for a family of four, so check that first. Leases are excluded.
  • Seeing it first: Tesla sells used cars online with no test drive, but you inspect the exact car at pickup before signing and can walk away. The Buffalo Grove Model 3 is flagged "available to view" at the store. Book a free test drive of a new Model 3 and Model Y at Tesla Orland Park to learn the car.
  • Financing: Tesla's low-rate loan (about 2.49% now) is only on new Model Y trims. For a used car, get a pre-approval from your credit union before you click Order so Tesla's rate has something to beat.
  • Warranty on a Tesla used car: whatever is left of the 4-year/50,000-mile factory warranty, then Tesla's 1-year/10,000-mile used warranty. Battery and drive unit: 8 years from the original sale (100,000 to 120,000 miles depending on trim). Every row shows the battery date.
  • Winter range: expect about 30% less range in January. Model 3 RWD cars have LFP batteries, which are very durable and like being charged to 100%, but they lose the most range in the cold. The Long Range cars have heat pumps and bigger packs.
  • Skip Full Self-Driving. It's $99 a month if you ever want to try it. Don't pay for it up front.
  • Home charging: budget about $500 to $1,200 for a 240-volt outlet or wall charger in the garage. That's the step most first-time buyers skip and then regret.
  • Illinois EV plates cost $251 a year instead of $151, roughly offset by gas savings in the first month or two.

Sources: Tesla.com pre-owned inventory and order pages (Oct 11, Oct 16 and Oct 18, 2026); CarsDirect Model Y and Model 3 pricing and lease/finance offers (checked Nov 5, 2026; leases expire Nov 30); Illinois EPA Electric Vehicle Rebate Program page (cycle Aug 1 to Dec 31, 2026); Tesla Pre-Owned Vehicle Limited Warranty (North America, 2025); TeslaTracker resale curves; Not a Tesla App lease vs. buy guide (May 2026).
